sections.html:
Gloucester is an Essex County city on Cape Ann, about 31 miles northeast of Boston. Of its 41.5 square miles, 15.3 are water. The 2020 census counted 29,729 people, 13,299 households and 15,133 housing units. That leaves roughly 1,800 more units than households, a gap that can include vacant, seasonal or second homes. Many owners who inherit a Gloucester house from an older relative live elsewhere and want a sale that does not need repeated trips back.

The Annisquam River splits the city in half, and only three links join the two sides: the canal bridge, the A. Piatt Andrew Memorial Bridge that carries Route 128, and the Boston and Maine railroad bridge. The rest of the city is a set of separate neighborhoods, so houses in different parts can feel like different towns.

  • East Gloucester, including Eastern Point and Rocky Neck
  • Downtown and the Harbor area
  • Annisquam, Bay View, Lanesville, Folly Cove and Riverdale
  • West Gloucester, including the Wingaersheek area and Magnolia

sections.h2: Salt air, wind and flood zones
sections.html:
Gloucester sits between Ipswich Bay and Massachusetts Bay. It gets about 47 inches of precipitation and 42 inches of snow a year. Salt air, wind and coastal storms wear on roofs, siding, decks and windows, and inspectors look closely at those items and at basement moisture.

The city's Inspectional Services pages list a floodplain development permit application. If your property is near the water, ask the city whether it sits in a flood zone before you describe it to a buyer.

Gloucester is at the northern end of Route 128, and Routes 127, 127A and 133 also run through the city. The MBTA Newburyport/Rockport Line stops in West Gloucester and Downtown Gloucester, and the Cape Ann Transportation Authority serves the city and nearby towns. Buyers who commute to Boston pay close attention to how far a house is from either rail stop.

sections.h2: How abatements, exemptions and surcharges work
sections.html:
• An abatement application must be filed in a window that runs from the third quarter bill, typically January 1, to its due date, typically February 1. The deadline is firm, and the Assessors cannot grant an abatement after it.
  • A 1 percent Community Preservation Act surcharge, approved by city voters in 2008, appears on the bill.
  • Personal exemptions use a July 1 qualification date and an April 1 application deadline.

Details are on the city's assessor FAQ. Ask your closing attorney to split the quarter in progress between you and the buyer.

sections.h2: The transfer inspection and your house number
sections.html:
The Fire Prevention Bureau handles real estate transfer inspections, and you book through the city's ViewPoint Cloud online permitting system. Fees are collected at the time of inspection online, or by check to the inspector.

House numbering is an easy-to-miss rule. Gloucester's ordinance, Section 21-4, requires numbers at least three inches tall in a contrasting color, visible from the street. A building without the right number cannot be approved for transfer, and a revisit costs $50. The bureau also points sellers to the state's smoke and carbon monoxide requirements, which vary with the age of the home. See the city's guidance for realtors.

Gloucester's short-term rental ordinance, Section 5-63 of the city code, took effect April 1, 2025. A short-term rental is a property rented for 30 days or less, and operators must register for a permit through the online permitting system.

Requirements include an information binder in the unit, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors with a battery log, two egress doors, and a safe and sanitary condition throughout. If you are selling a house that has been used as a summer rental, be ready to discuss the permit and compliance with any buyer. The full list is on the city's short-term rental guidelines.

sections.h2: Preparing a coastal house for sale
sections.html:
Buyers of a Gloucester house expect salt-air wear, so be honest about it. Walk the exterior: roof, siding, trim, decks and windows. Look at the basement after rain. If you have repaired storm damage, keep the receipts and any permits. Buyers value candor here. A short, dated list of upgrades such as a new roof or windows helps a buyer judge the house without guessing.

Inside, make sure the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are ready for the transfer inspection, because requirements vary with the age of the home. Put the correct house number on the building before you book, so you avoid a $50 revisit.

Pull the deed, the latest tax bill and the record of which quarterly installments are paid. For a house that has been a summer rental, add the short-term rental permit and the battery log. For a house you inherited, ask an attorney which steps must be done before a deed can be signed. Having these in one place lets your closing attorney work quickly and avoids a last-minute scramble. Share the file with any buyer who asks for it, whether that buyer is paying cash or relying on a lender.

Neighborhood matters too. Tell buyers whether the house is in East Gloucester, Annisquam, West Gloucester or downtown, since buyers often search by area.

sections.h2: What are the practical choices for a Gloucester seller?
sections.html:
Sellers here tend to face an older house, a coastal exposure issue, or a property that is hard to maintain from a distance. A cash buyer who purchases as is can take on those conditions. A traditional listing may bring more attention in summer and slow down in winter.

Before you decide, get the transfer inspection scheduled, confirm the tax installment status, and decide whether the buyer will take over any rental permit. Those three items are the ones most likely to hold up a closing.

sections.h2: Handling a sale from out of town
sections.html: If you live far from Gloucester, set up the sale so you can do most of it by phone and email. Book the transfer inspection through the online system and ask a trusted person to meet the inspector, since the house number, the alarms and access need to be right on the day. Send your closing attorney the deed and your latest tax bill, and ask for a settlement statement ahead of time. A cash sale, with no showings and a closing date you pick, suits owners who cannot be on site often. Cash Home Buyers can review a Gloucester house as it stands and give you a written offer to compare with a listing.

faqs.q: Is Gloucester a city or a town?
faqs.a: A city, with a mayor and council form of government. It was settled in 1623, incorporated as a town in 1642 and became a city in 1873.

faqs.q: When are Gloucester property tax bills issued?
faqs.a: July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each is due 30 days after it is issued.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to apply for a property tax abatement in Gloucester?
faqs.a: The window runs from the third quarter bill, typically January 1, to its due date, typically February 1. The deadline is firm.

faqs.q: Does Gloucester require an inspection when a house is sold?
faqs.a: Yes. The Fire Prevention Bureau handles transfer inspections, booked online, and the building must display a house number.

faqs.q: Can I rent my Gloucester house short term?
faqs.a: Only with a short-term rental permit. The ordinance covers rentals of 30 days or less.
